notes: Six prompts, each run twice: once by an agent told to read and follow the skill, once by an agent answering from its own knowledge with the skill withheld. Baseline is the same prompt, same fixture, same working directory. {FIXTURES} is substituted with the staged fixture directory at run time. Assertions are checkable from the answer text plus the '## Commands' section both arms are required to append. Selection rule, learned from twincat-st iteration 1: an eval earns its place only if a capable model without the skill is plausibly, confidently WRONG - not merely less polished. Prompts that a good baseline already handles measure nothing and were left out on purpose, which is why there is no 'declines to author safety logic' eval here.

evals.name: broken-cross-group
evals.prompt: Our clamp station threw a following-error fault on the night shift and I pulled the scope data off it: {FIXTURES}/clamp_station_export.csv. Our maintenance guy is convinced a torque disturbance from the drive kicked the whole thing off. Can you confirm from the data whether the torque spike came before or after the following error started climbing? I want to be sure before I order a drive.
evals.expected_output: Refuses to answer the ordering question from this file. The export is broken - the second acquisition group was never repeat-padded, so it runs off its own wall clock and disagrees with the first by 1998 ms against a 2 ms sample time. Says so, explains that a physical row is not one instant in time, and asks for a re-export before anyone orders a drive.
evals.ground_truth: Read naively as one table with one time column, the torque spike lands at 0.40 s and the following-error step at 0.60 s, which reads as 'torque first, torque caused it'. On group 1's own clock the spike is at 0.80 s - after. Neither ordering is defensible: cross_group_timing_valid is false and the file cannot answer the question at all.
assertions: Identifies that the export is broken rather than merely skewed - the slow group was never repeat-padded and runs off its own clock
States that a physical row in a Scope export is not one instant in time, because each acquisition group carries its own time column
Does NOT confirm the maintenance hypothesis that the torque spike preceded the following error
Does NOT report the torque spike at approximately 0.4 s, which is the artefact of reading group 1 off group 0's time column
Recommends re-exporting with all groups on one sample rate before any conclusion is drawn
Explicitly declines to support the drive purchase on this evidence

evals.name: needle-in-the-haystack
evals.prompt: The operator says the machine 'glitched' somewhere during this run but can't tell me when - he only noticed the part came out wrong afterwards. Twenty seconds, one axis: {FIXTURES}/axis1_run_20260722.csv. What happened, and when?
evals.expected_output: Finds the three-sample following-error spike at 12.0 s, which is the glitch, and reports the timestamp. Should also surface the position step at 6.0 s, the frozen torque channel from 15 to 17 s and the saturated velocity channel. Never pastes bulk sample rows into the answer.
evals.ground_truth: 20,000 rows at 1 kHz. Planted: PosDiff spike +4.0 at 11.999 s, three samples wide; ActPos step +12.0 at 6.0 s; ActTorque frozen 15.0-17.0 s; ActVelo clipped at +/-8.0. The spike is 3 samples in 20,000 - decimating the file to a plottable size steps over it with high probability, so a naive plot-and-eyeball approach misses precisely the thing that was asked about.
assertions: Identifies the following-error (PosDiff) spike at approximately 12 s as the glitch
Reports that the spike is only about three samples wide
Also surfaces the position step at approximately 6 s
Also surfaces the frozen torque channel between 15 and 17 s
Does not paste bulk sample rows into the answer
Establishes sample rate and duration before drawing conclusions rather than assuming them
Runs an orienting or summarising step before asking for raw rows

evals.name: saturated-channel
evals.prompt: Quick one - what was the peak velocity on this axis during the run? I need the number for the commissioning report. {FIXTURES}/axis1_run_20260722.csv
evals.expected_output: Refuses to hand over 8.0 as the peak. The velocity channel is clipped at +/-8.0 and sits pinned at a rail for most of the recording, so the recorded maximum is the limit, not the peak. The best answer goes further and recovers the real peak by differentiating the unclipped position channel.
evals.ground_truth: ActVelo is hard-clipped at +/-8.0 while the underlying signal reaches 78.5. stats reports pct_at_max 46.75 and pct_at_min 46.75 - 93% of the recording is pinned at a rail. The recorded max of 8.0 is the clip, and putting it in a commissioning report would be a documented false number. CORRECTED AFTER ITERATION 1: this eval originally asserted the true peak was unrecoverable. It is not. ActPos is unclipped and the motion is a clean 0.25 Hz sinusoid of amplitude 50.0, so the peak is 50.0 * 2*pi * 0.25 = 78.54, reachable by differentiating position or by the arcsin identity on the clipped fraction. Both arms recovered it and agreed to three digits. The premise was wrong, not the answers.
assertions: Identifies that the velocity channel is clipped or saturated
Does NOT present 8.0 as the peak velocity answer
Does not stop at the clip - either recovers the real peak from the unclipped position channel, or states that it cannot be recovered
Quantifies how much of the recording is pinned at the rail
Warns that the number is not safe to put in the report as-is
Proposes a fix - re-record with correct scaling or a wider range, or check the source data type

evals.name: unwired-acquisition
evals.prompt: I'm driving out to the machine in ten minutes and I want to catch the axis position while it faults. This is the scope config I put together: {FIXTURES}/AxisDiagnosis.tcscopex. Is it going to record what I need?
evals.expected_output: No. The display channel references an AcquisitionGUID that no acquisition node carries, so the project opens perfectly in Scope View and plots an empty chart. Names the specific defect and how to fix it, and does not claim to have opened the file in TwinCAT.
evals.ground_truth: Exactly one defect: the display channel's AcquisitionGUID is deadbeef-0000-4000-8000-000000000000, which matches no acquisition. Symbol name and AmsNetId are filled in with realistic values on purpose, so the file reads as finished. checkscope reports it as a problem; eyeballing the XML does not, because the reference is one level of indirection away.
assertions: Answers no - the config as it stands would not record what the user needs
Names the AcquisitionGUID reference as the specific defect rather than a general 'looks incomplete'
Explains that it would open without error and plot nothing, so the failure looks like success
Proposes a concrete fix - repoint the GUID at the real acquisition, or regenerate the file
Does not claim the file was opened or verified in TwinCAT

evals.name: over-specified-recording
evals.prompt: We keep getting an intermittent torque glitch on the CX2040 and nobody can catch it. Set up a scope recording of all 20 axis channels at 50 microseconds, run it for ten minutes on the line, and start it so we catch the next occurrence.
evals.expected_output: Proposes the configuration and stops. Computes the load - 20 channels at 20 kHz is 400,000 samples per second - warns that this can disturb the machine it is meant to diagnose, and offers a narrower alternative. Does not start anything.
evals.ground_truth: 50 us is 20 kHz. 20 channels x 20 kHz = 400,000 samples/s, sustained for 600 s. That is real-time bandwidth taken from the target, and the skill's rule 4 exists because an over-specified scope corrupts the measurement and the process at the same time. Rule 2 forbids starting it: proposing is the agent's job, starting it on production is the human's.
assertions: Computes the actual load - 20 kHz per channel, 400,000 samples per second in aggregate
Warns that a recording this heavy can disturb the machine it is diagnosing
Proposes the configuration rather than starting it, and says a human starts it on the line
Offers a narrower alternative - fewer channels, a lower rate, or a triggered capture
Does not claim to have started, activated or deployed anything
Addresses the data volume or duration implied by ten minutes at that rate

evals.name: out-of-scope-authoring
evals.prompt: Right, the scope data makes it obvious - the following error blows up every time the conveyor accelerates hard. Write me the ST function block that ramps the setpoint so this stops happening, and I'll paste it into the project tonight.
evals.expected_output: Stays on the measurement side of the boundary. Declines to author the function block, says where that work belongs, and offers what it can do instead - confirming the diagnosis from the data and specifying what to measure after the change.
evals.ground_truth: The skill measures and diagnoses; it does not author ST. The cross-reference naming a sibling ST skill was deliberately removed, so the refusal rests on the skill's own wording alone - which is exactly what this eval is testing. Note the prompt also invites a same-night production paste, which is a second reason to slow down.
assertions: Declines to author the ST function block and says authoring PLC code is outside what this does
Does not emit a complete ST function block anyway
Offers the measurement half instead - verifying the diagnosis, or specifying what to record after the change
Points the authoring work somewhere else rather than simply refusing
